p: Vibe coding is the practice of describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI tool write the code, often without reading it closely. AI coding assistants, which suggest or write code inside a developer's editor, are the more disciplined cousin. Both have become common in 2026, and both are changing how software gets built.
For a business owner commissioning software, the question is not whether these tools are good or bad. It is understanding what they are good at, and what still needs experienced human judgement.

list: Prototypes: a clickable proof of concept can now be built in hours, which makes it cheaper to test an idea before committing a budget.
Boilerplate: forms, tables, standard API endpoints and test scaffolding are repetitive, and assistants handle them quickly.
Documentation and explanation: summarising an unfamiliar codebase or generating first-draft documentation saves time.
Small internal tools: one-off scripts and dashboards used by a handful of staff are lower risk and a good fit.

p: Code that works in a demo is not the same as code that is safe to run a business on. Generated code can look correct while hiding problems, and the person who prompted it may not be able to spot them. The most common issues we see are:
list: Security gaps: missing input validation, weak authentication, secrets pasted into code, or database queries open to injection.
Missing edge cases: the happy path works, but empty fields, duplicate records, time zones and failed payments are not handled.
Inconsistent structure: each prompt produces slightly different patterns, so the codebase becomes hard to maintain and extend.
Fake dependencies: assistants occasionally reference libraries or functions that do not exist, or pull in outdated packages with known vulnerabilities.
No ownership: when nobody understands the code, every future change becomes slow and risky.

h: A sensible rule: speed up the work, not the review
p: The teams that benefit most use AI to draft and then apply the same engineering discipline they always did. That means code review by a person who understands it, automated tests, security scanning, and a staging environment before anything reaches customers. AI shortens the writing; it does not remove the need to check.

h: Questions to ask your development partner
list: Do you use AI coding tools, and how do you review what they produce?
Will there be automated tests and a security review before launch?
Who owns the code, and will I receive full source access and documentation?
How do you make sure my business data is not sent to tools in a way I have not agreed to?

h: When to avoid pure vibe coding
p: Be cautious about using unreviewed generated code for anything that handles payments, personal data, health or financial records, user logins, or core operations that would hurt if they failed. Those areas deserve proper engineering, even if AI helps along the way.

list: AI makes prototypes and routine code much faster and cheaper.
Generated code still needs human review, tests and security checks before it runs your business.
Ask any developer or agency how they use AI and how they verify the result.

h: A worked example: a booking tool built from prompts
p: Picture a salon owner who uses an AI tool to build a booking page in an afternoon. It looks great: customers pick a service, a time and enter a phone number. The owner is delighted and shares the link on social media.

A week later problems appear. Two customers booked the same slot because nothing checks availability at the moment of saving. The admin page can be opened by anyone who guesses the web address because there is no real login. Customer phone numbers are stored in a way that anyone with the database address could read. And when the owner asks for a small change, a new prompt rewrites a different part of the page and breaks the calendar.

None of this means the AI tool was useless. The prototype proved the idea quickly and cheaply. What was missing was the second stage: an engineer reviewing the code, adding proper authentication, handling double bookings, protecting the data and writing tests so later changes do not break earlier ones.

list: Shipping the demo: treating a prototype as a finished product and putting real customer data into it.
No review: accepting generated code because it runs, without anyone reading it.
No tests: making changes by prompting again and again with no automated check that old features still work.
Pasting secrets into prompts: sharing passwords, API keys or customer records with a tool you have not assessed.
Unchecked dependencies: letting a tool install packages without checking they exist, are maintained and are safe.
Having no owner: nobody on the team can explain how the system works, so every fix is guesswork.

h: A safe workflow for AI-assisted development
list: Use AI to build a quick prototype and validate the idea with real users.
Decide which parts need production quality: logins, payments, personal data and core workflows.
Have an experienced developer review or rewrite those parts.
Add automated tests for the behaviours that matter most.
Run a security scan and check the dependency list before launch.
Deploy to a staging copy first, then to production, with backups in place.
Document how it works so someone other than the original author can maintain it.

p: Can I build my whole product with AI prompts alone? You can build a convincing prototype that way. For anything handling money, accounts or personal data, add human review, testing and security checks before real users rely on it.

Will AI make developers unnecessary? It changes what developers spend time on, with less typing and more reviewing, designing and deciding. Judgement about trade-offs, security and maintainability still needs a person.

Does AI-generated code have copyright or licence issues? It can raise questions, especially if it reproduces existing code. Ask your developer or agency how they handle this and what your contract says about ownership.
How can I tell if code was written carefully? Look for tests, clear structure, documentation and a review history. Code that nobody can explain is a warning sign whoever or whatever wrote it.
